rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1 and 5 - own field experiment with a fuzzy-logic IoT irrigation controller on apple trees in eastern Morocco, summer 2022 and winter 2023, comparing an SPIS-controlled zone with a timer-controlled zone.
rows.notes: The study reports water saving (about 61%) and energy saving (about 46%) of the smart scheduling system relative to a manual timer over 10 days, and that soil moisture tracked the 30% target. It does not measure any climate-risk, drought resilience or adaptation outcome; water saving is at most a precondition for the adaptation/resilience effect implied by the claim's function.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1, 5 - own field experiment in eastern Morocco (zone A with SPIS vs zone B with manual timer), 10 days in summer 2022 and 10 in winter 2023. Q2: Section 5.3 - flow-meter measured water use; SPIS applied 51.6 mm versus 110 mm by the farmer's timer, a water saving of nearly 61% over 10 days, plus about 46% lower power consumption. Q4: Section 5.1, Fig. 14(d), Fig. 15 - soil moisture measured hourly and shown tracking the 30% set point; irrigation withheld during high temperature/irradiance (high ET) periods; applied water (5.29 mm/day) compared with Penman-Monteith ET (5.31 mm/day), i.e. the mechanism of matching applied water to crop demand is measured. Q8: Section 2.2.1 - authors state a single soil moisture sensor was used in zone A and that further subdivision of the field and sensor-placement work is needed to ensure generalizability of results across the entire field; Section 5.2 notes the system is still being expanded to larger areas. Q9: Section 5.3 - water saving reported as 61% (plus or minus 2%).
rows.notes: Q3 no: the saving is established by flow-meter comparison only; the ET comparison checks adequacy of applied water, not an independent estimate of the saving. Q5/Q6 no: one field, one crop (apple), irrigated area about 100 m2 per zone. Q7 no: the 30% soil-moisture threshold for apple and sensor calibration are design settings, not stated as requirements for the saving to occur. Comparison is against a farmer-set timer applying 11 mm/day; duration only 10 days per season. The plus/minus 2% is unexplained in origin.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1 and 5 - own field experiment with the SPIS on apple trees in eastern Morocco.
rows.notes: The study measures water and energy consumption and soil moisture only. No yield, growth or product-quality data are reported; statements that plants are kept 'in better condition, no stress' and 'optimal hydration' are asserted from soil moisture tracking, not measured crop productivity. Maintaining soil moisture is a precondition for the claimed productivity effect.

notes: Full text appears complete. Experiment: single apple orchard, zones A (SPIS, drip, impulse solenoid) and B (manual commercial timer, classic solenoid), ~100 m2 irrigated each, 10 days in September 2022 and 10 days in January 2023. Outcomes limited to applied water, energy, soil moisture and ET comparison; no crop outcomes.
